## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Describe a numeric column, or part of it, with statistical functions such as AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STDEV.S, MIN, MAX, and PERCENTILE.INC, and show the shape of its distribution with a histogram.
2. Calculate conditional totals, counts, and averages with SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIFS, MINIFS, and MAXIFS, and prove that a summary is complete with a control total.
3. Build PivotTables and PivotCharts from an Excel Table that summarize data across two or more dimensions, and choose a chart that fits the question.
4. Create calculated fields for margins and ratios, and explain why a calculated field works on totals rather than on individual rows.
5. Explain a change between two periods by drilling down, comparing, and decomposing it into price, volume, mix, and cost effects, and communicate the finding.
6. Build a pre-closing trial balance and a common-size income statement from the general ledger.
:::

## Opening Scenario {.unnumbered}

InvoiceLines is ready, and the controller has three requests for the quarterly management meeting. First, she wants a profile of what Charles River billed in fiscal 2026: how many invoice lines, how large they were, how widely they varied, and a total that ties to the figures she already trusts. Second, she wants revenue and gross margin by product line and quarter, so that the management team can see how the Furniture decline compares with the company's other lines, together with the year's income statement from the ledger. Third, and most important, she wants the answer to the question she asked in your first week: why did the Furniture margin fall from the third quarter to the fourth?

The earlier chapters gave you a clean, reconciled table and a clue, the Furniture Seasonal Promotion, whose orders were still being invoiced after it ended. This chapter gives you the tools to describe what happened and then to explain why: statistical functions, conditional aggregation, PivotTables, and a margin bridge that breaks a change into its causes.



## Descriptive and Diagnostic Analytics in Accounting

Chapter 1 introduced four types of analytics. Descriptive analytics answers the question "what happened?" by summarizing historical data into totals, averages, counts, distributions, and comparisons. Diagnostic analytics answers "why did it happen?" by drilling into those summaries, comparing them with an expectation, and breaking a change into its components. In accounting, descriptive analytics is not a warm-up for the real analysis. Comparative financial statements, budget-to-actual reports, aging schedules, and key performance indicators are all descriptive analytics, and they are much of what accountants produce. Diagnostic analytics is what happens when one of those reports shows something that nobody expected and someone has to explain it. The competency framework of the Institute of Management Accountants (IMA) includes a domain dedicated to data analytics, reflecting how central these skills have become to the profession (IMA, 2025).

This chapter moves from one type to the other, using four families of tools. Statistical functions reduce a column to a single number, such as the average or the median billed amount of an invoice line. Conditional aggregation functions, such as SUMIFS, calculate totals, counts, and averages for the rows that meet criteria you define. PivotTables summarize data across two or more dimensions at once, such as revenue by product line and quarter. Finally, a margin bridge decomposes the change in a measure between two periods into effects that add up exactly to the change. The first three describe; the last one explains. Along the way, you will chart the results and build the year's income statement from the general ledger. By the end of the chapter, you will have used all four families of tools to answer the controller's question.


## Summary Statistics

A statistical function reduces a column of values to one number that describes the column as a whole. No single measure tells the whole story, so analysts combine measures of the center of the data, of its spread, and of its extremes.

### Central Tendency

`AVERAGE(range)` returns the arithmetic mean, the sum of the values divided by their number. It is the most familiar summary measure, but a few very large values pull it upward. `MEDIAN(range)` returns the middle value when the values are sorted, or the average of the two middle values when their number is even. Because it depends only on position, the median is not affected by how extreme the largest values are.

The gap between the two is informative. When the mean is well above the median, the distribution is skewed to the right: most values are moderate, and a minority of large values pulls the average up. Accounting populations are usually shaped this way. For the Charles River invoice lines of fiscal 2026, the average line is about half again as large as the median line, so the typical line is smaller than the average suggests, and a relatively small share of large lines carries a large share of the revenue. When you report a "typical" transaction, the median is usually the better measure, and when you report a total or plan a test of dollar amounts, the mean and the large values matter more.

### Dispersion and Extremes

The standard deviation measures how widely values are spread around their mean. `STDEV.S(range)` treats the values as a sample, a subset drawn from a larger population, and divides by the number of values minus one. `STDEV.P(range)` treats them as the complete population and divides by the number of values. The distinction matters for small samples, such as an audit sample of a few dozen items. For thousands of invoice lines, the two results differ by a fraction of a percent, and analysts commonly use STDEV.S. A standard deviation is easiest to interpret relative to the mean: two cost centers with the same average monthly spending are very different to manage if one varies by a few percent from month to month and the other by a third.

`MIN(range)` and `MAX(range)` return the smallest and largest values. They are summary measures, but they are also data checks. A negative or zero amount where none should exist, or a maximum far above the rest of the data, is worth a look before any other statistic is trusted. In the fiscal 2026 invoice lines, the smallest line is under two dollars and the largest is not a piece of furniture but a design services engagement, a reminder that the lines mix very different kinds of sales. `PERCENTILE.INC(range, k)`, which you used in Chapter 4 to set the large-line threshold, returns the value below which a share k of the values falls, and the top tenth of the fiscal 2026 lines carries nearly a third of the year's revenue.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
Summary statistics can hide what the data looks like. Anscombe (1973) constructed four small data sets that share the same means, standard deviations, and fitted regression line (the kind of line Chapter 7 fits to data) but look completely different when they are plotted. A statistic of a mixed population can also describe none of its members: the average fiscal 2026 invoice line falls between the small Accessories lines and the large design-services lines, and it resembles neither. Before relying on a statistic, sort, filter, or chart the data it summarizes, and calculate the statistic separately for groups that behave differently.
:::

### Statistics for Part of a Table

Most questions concern part of a table, such as one fiscal year or one product line. AVERAGEIFS, MINIFS, and MAXIFS accept criteria, as SUMIFS does, but MEDIAN, STDEV.S, and PERCENTILE.INC do not, and Excel has no MEDIANIFS. The FILTER function fills the gap. `FILTER(array, include)` returns the rows of an array for which a condition is true, and any statistical function can then summarize the result:

```
=MEDIAN(FILTER(InvoiceLines[LineTotal],InvoiceLines[FiscalYear]=2026))
```

FILTER is available in Microsoft 365 and Excel 2021 or later, the same versions the Power Query tutorials already require. If no row meets the condition, FILTER returns the error #CALC!, which is a signal to check the condition before trusting the result.


## Conditional Aggregation and Control Totals

You have already used SUMIFS and COUNTIFS, in Chapter 4 to count the lines above a threshold and in Chapter 5 to total the Furniture revenue by quarter. The pattern is the same in every function of the family. The first argument of SUMIFS, AVERAGEIFS, MINIFS, and MAXIFS is the range to aggregate, and COUNTIFS, which only counts, has none. Pairs of arguments follow, each a criteria range and a criterion, and a row is included only when it meets every criterion. A comparison is written as text joined to a value, as in `">"&LargeLineThreshold`.

Criteria are easier to maintain in cells than in formulas. The formula

```
=SUMIFS(InvoiceLines[LineTotal],InvoiceLines[ItemGroup],$A12,InvoiceLines[FiscalYear],ReportYear)
```

takes the item group from column A of its own row and the fiscal year from a named cell. Copied down a column of item groups, it returns each group's revenue, and changing ReportYear updates every row. The mixed reference `$A12`, which you learned in Chapter 4, keeps the formula pointed at column A when it is copied.

Conditional aggregation has one dangerous property: it fails silently. A SUMIFS whose criterion is misspelled, such as "Furnture", returns zero rather than an error, and a list of categories typed by hand can simply leave one out. The defense is a control total, an independently calculated total that the parts of a summary must add up to. You have used control totals since Chapter 4, when you compared the sum of the invoice lines with the sum of the invoice subtotals. In a summary by category, the control total is the total of the whole population for the same criteria, and the difference between it and the sum of the categories must be zero. Auditors apply the same discipline when they foot a schedule, adding its columns, and cross-foot it, adding its rows, before relying on it.


## Charting Descriptive Results

A table of statistics describes a distribution in numbers. A chart shows its shape, and a well-chosen chart lets a reader see a trend, a comparison, or an outlier at a glance. The Watch out box above makes the same point from the other side: statistics that look alike can describe data that look nothing alike. Excel's charts are on the Insert tab, and the first decision is which kind of chart answers the question. @tbl-06-01 matches the common questions of descriptive analysis to the charts that answer them.

| Question | Chart | Accounting example |
|---|---|---|
| How do categories compare? | Column or bar chart, sorted by value | Revenue by product line |
| How does a measure change over time? | Line chart | Monthly revenue or margin |
| What does a total consist of? | Stacked column chart | Revenue by segment within each quarter |
| How are values distributed? | Histogram | The number of invoice lines in each range of amounts |
| How do two measures relate? | Scatter chart | Commission expense against revenue by month |
| How did one total become another? | Waterfall chart | The change in margin from one quarter to the next |

: Charts for common descriptive questions {#tbl-06-01}

### Histograms

A histogram divides the range of a measure into bins of equal width, such as line totals from $0 to $1,000, from $1,000 to $2,000, and so on, and draws a bar for the number of values in each bin. It is the chart that shows the shape of a distribution, such as the right skew of the invoice lines. Excel draws one directly from a column of values with Insert > Insert Statistic Chart > Histogram, and the bin width can be set on the horizontal axis with Format Axis (Microsoft, 2026c). That chart counts every value in the range it is given, however. To count only the lines of one fiscal year, you can instead build a frequency table with COUNTIFS, one row for each bin, and chart it as a column chart with no gap between the bars, which is what Tutorial 6.1 does.

### PivotCharts

A PivotChart is a chart built on a PivotTable. It shows the PivotTable's current layout, so filtering the PivotTable, or clicking a slicer connected to it, filters the chart too, and a refresh updates both. Insert a PivotChart from PivotTable Analyze > PivotChart, or build a PivotTable and its chart in one step with Insert > PivotChart.

### Designing a Chart That Tells the Truth

A few rules keep a chart honest and easy to read. The length of a bar represents its value, so the value axis of a column or bar chart should start at zero. When a line chart or a waterfall chart needs a truncated axis to make small differences visible, as the bridge in Tutorial 6.3 does, say so in the title or a note. Sort bars by value unless their categories have a natural order, such as months. Label the chart with what it shows and what it means, remove decoration such as 3-D effects and heavy gridlines, and use color to mean something, never as the only way a message is carried, for the reasons Chapter 4 gave for conditional formatting.


{{< include _tutorial-01.qmd >}}


## PivotTables

The summaries in Tutorial 6.1 work, but you had to design the layout, type the categories, and write a formula for every cell. A PivotTable builds the layout for you. You choose which fields to place in its rows and columns and which to summarize, and Excel creates a cross-tabulation, a summary with a cell for every combination of the row and column items and totals for every row and column. Domino et al. (2021) built a teaching case around them, emphasizing how quickly they condense a large, complex data set into reports that address managers' questions. That speed has a cost: a PivotTable is as easy to misread as it is to build, so this section covers both how to build one and how to check it.

### Creating a PivotTable

Select any cell in an Excel Table and choose Insert > PivotTable, and then From Table/Range if Excel offers a choice. The dialog shows the Table's name as the source. A Table is the right source because the PivotTable then covers every row the Table holds, including rows added the next time the query is refreshed. Place the PivotTable on a new worksheet, so that it cannot overwrite anything.

Excel creates an empty PivotTable and opens the PivotTable Fields pane, which lists every column of the Table as a field. Below the list are four areas, and the field you drag into each area plays the role shown in @fig-06-03. The Rows and Columns areas define the categories down the side and across the top. The Values area holds the fields to summarize. The Filters area limits the whole PivotTable to the rows that meet a condition, such as a single fiscal year, without changing the source.

![How the PivotTable Fields Areas Build a PivotTable.](/visuals/svg/fig-06-03-pivottable-areas.svg){#fig-06-03 fig-alt="A diagram of the PivotTable Fields pane next to the PivotTable it produces from the InvoiceLines Table. In the pane, the LineTotal, ItemGroup, FiscalYear, and Period fields are checked, and the four areas hold FiscalYear in Filters, Period in Columns, ItemGroup in Rows, and Sum of LineTotal in Values, each marked with a number from 1 to 4. The PivotTable shows the FiscalYear filter set to 2026, the four quarters of 2026 and a Grand Total across the top, the five item groups and a Grand Total down the side, and the sum of the line totals in every cell. The same numbers mark the parts of the PivotTable that each area produces, and a legend explains them."}

### Summarizing Values

A numeric field in the Values area is summed by default, and a text field is counted. To change the calculation, click the field in the Values area and choose Value Field Settings, where you can choose Count, Average, Max, Min, and others, give the field a custom name, and set its number format with the Number Format button. Counting an ID column, such as SalesInvoiceLineID, counts rows, which is the PivotTable equivalent of COUNTIFS. When you place more than one field in the Values area, Excel adds a field called Σ Values to the Columns area, and dragging it to the Rows area stacks the measures vertically instead, which is often easier to read.

### Grouping by Period

PivotTables can group a date field into months, quarters, and years: right-click a date in the PivotTable, choose Group, and select the units. Date grouping follows the calendar, and it requires every value in the field to be a real date, so a single text date, the problem Chapter 5 warned about, prevents it. For Charles River, whose fiscal year is the calendar year, calendar quarters and fiscal quarters coincide. InvoiceLines already carries FiscalYear, FiscalQuarter, and Period columns, however, and using them keeps the PivotTable consistent with every other analysis of the table. For an organization whose fiscal year does not follow the calendar, period columns calculated during preparation are the only reliable choice.

### Calculated Fields

A calculated field is a field you define inside a PivotTable with a formula that uses other fields. It is how a PivotTable shows a measure that is not a column of the source, such as a margin percentage. Choose PivotTable Analyze > Fields, Items, & Sets > Calculated Field, give the field a name, and write its formula using the field names. The essential point is how the formula is evaluated. Microsoft's documentation explains that a calculated field's formula operates on the sums of the fields it uses, not on individual records (Microsoft, 2026a). For each cell of the PivotTable, Excel first sums each field over the rows behind the cell and then applies the formula to those sums. A margin percentage defined as `=(LineTotal-StdCostAmount)/LineTotal` is therefore the total margin divided by the total revenue of each cell, which is exactly the weighted margin an accountant wants.

The same rule explains why a margin needs a cost column that is already extended. InvoiceLines carries each item's StandardCost, the cost of one unit, and summing a unit cost over many lines produces a meaningless number. Tutorial 6.2 therefore adds StdCostAmount, the quantity multiplied by the standard cost, to the query, and the calculated field uses that.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
Because a calculated field works on sums, a formula that multiplies two fields gives the wrong answer. A calculated field defined as `=Quantity*UnitPrice` multiplies the total quantity by the total of the unit prices, which is not revenue at any level of the PivotTable. Multiply values row by row in the source, as a custom column in Power Query or a calculated column in the Table, and let the PivotTable sum the product. Ratios and differences of totals, such as margins and averages per unit, are what calculated fields do well.
:::

### Show Values As

The same value field can be displayed in different ways without changing the numbers behind it. Right-click a value in the PivotTable, choose Show Values As, and pick a calculation. @tbl-06-02 lists the options accountants use most, with the descriptions Microsoft gives for them (Microsoft, 2026b), and @fig-06-04 shows one PivotTable displayed three ways.

| Show Values As option | What it displays | Accounting use |
|---|---|---|
| % of Grand Total | Each value as a share of the grand total | Each segment and product line's share of the year's revenue |
| % of Column Total | Each value as a share of its column's total | The product mix within each quarter |
| % of Row Total | Each value as a share of its row's total | How a product line's revenue is spread across the quarters |
| Difference From | The difference from a base item, such as the previous period | The dollar change from one quarter to the next |
| % Difference From | The percentage difference from a base item | Growth or decline from the previous quarter or year |
| Running Total In | A running total across the base field | Year-to-date revenue by month |

: Show Values As options for accounting summaries {#tbl-06-02}

![One PivotTable Shown Three Ways with Show Values As.](/visuals/svg/fig-06-04-show-values-as.svg){#fig-06-04 fig-alt="Three small PivotTables side by side, each showing the five item groups and a Grand Total for the third and fourth quarters of fiscal 2026. The first shows Sum of LineTotal with no calculation, the second shows each group's share of the quarter with % of Column Total, and the third shows the change from the previous quarter with % Difference From. The Furniture cell for the fourth quarter is outlined in all three, showing a lower revenue, a smaller share of the quarter, and a decline from the third quarter."}

### Refreshing and Referencing a PivotTable

A PivotTable summarizes a copy of its source, called the pivot cache, so it does not change when the source changes. After a query refresh, the PivotTable must be refreshed too, and Data > Refresh All does both. A formula that refers to a PivotTable should use GETPIVOTDATA, which Excel writes for you when you type an equal sign and click a value in the PivotTable. `GETPIVOTDATA` identifies the value by its field and items, such as the Sum of LineTotal for Period 2026-Q4, rather than by its cell address, so it keeps returning the right value when the PivotTable's layout changes. Slicers, which you used on a Table in Chapter 4, filter PivotTables in the same way, and one slicer can control several PivotTables built from the same source.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
A PivotTable reports what is in its source, including rows that should not be in the analysis. In the Part I case, you found that a summary of the general ledger by quarter shows nonsensical fourth-quarter revenue and cost of goods sold, because the year-end closing entry debits the revenue accounts and credits the cost of goods sold accounts on the last day of the year. Before you summarize GLEntry by period, filter out the JournalEntry rows of the closing entries, or place SourceDocumentType in the Filters area and select the source documents your question concerns. The same caution applies to any source: know which rows it contains before you trust its totals.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
A common task in the monthly close is a flux analysis, in which the accounting team compares each account's balance with the previous period and with the same period of the previous year, and explains every change above a threshold. A PivotTable of the ledger by account and period, with a Difference From or % Difference From value field and a conditional formatting rule for the threshold, produces the list of changes to explain in a few minutes. The explanations still require someone who knows the business, and they are what reviewers and auditors read.
:::

## From the Ledger to the Financial Statements

The PivotTables in this chapter start from the invoice lines, the detail behind revenue. The financial statements start from the general ledger. As Chapter 2 explained, a trial balance lists every account with its balance at a date, and the statements are prepared from it. Chapter 3 showed that the Charles River database has no trial balance table: you produce one by grouping the GLEntry rows by account and summing their debits and credits. This section shows how to do that in Excel and how to turn the result into an income statement.

### Building a Trial Balance with Power Query

GLEntry holds hundreds of thousands of rows, which is more than you want in a worksheet only to add them up. Power Query's Group By command, on the Transform tab of the Power Query Editor, summarizes the rows before they are loaded. You choose one or more columns to group by, such as AccountID, and one or more aggregations, such as the sum of Debit and the sum of Credit. The Advanced option of the Group By dialog allows several aggregations at once. The result has one row for each account, which a merge with the Account Table then labels with the account's number, name, type, and subtype.

Two choices decide what the trial balance shows. The first is the cutoff: only the rows posted on or before the reporting date belong in it. The second is the closing entries. At the end of each year, closing entries move the balances of the revenue and expense accounts to retained earnings, which leaves those accounts at zero. A trial balance prepared before the current year's closing entries, a pre-closing trial balance, therefore shows the current year's revenue and expenses, because the earlier years' closing entries have already cleared the earlier years' amounts. For Charles River at the end of fiscal 2026, that means every row posted through December 31, 2026, except the two 2026 closing entries: JE-2026-000296, which you met in the Part I case, and JE-2026-000297, which moves the year's net income to retained earnings. The balance sheet accounts, which are never closed, carry their balances forward from the opening balance entry of January 2024.

In the loaded trial balance, a calculated column subtracts each account's credits from its debits to give its balance, and two more columns place a positive balance in a DebitBalance column and a negative one in a CreditBalance column. The two columns must have equal totals, which is the trial balance's control total.

### From the Trial Balance to the Income Statement

The Account Table's AccountSubType column groups the accounts into the lines of the statements: Operating Revenue, Contra Revenue, COGS, Operating Expense, and so on. SUMIFS on the trial balance then produces each line of the income statement, with the sign reversed for revenue, whose normal balance is a credit:

```
=-SUMIFS(TrialBalance[Balance],TrialBalance[AccountSubType],"Operating Revenue")
```

A common-size statement expresses every line as a percentage of net revenue, which makes the structure of the statement easy to read and to compare with another period or another company: gross margin, operating expenses, and net income each become a share of every dollar of revenue. Comparing the same lines across years is called horizontal analysis, and comparing lines within one year, as a common-size statement does, is called vertical analysis. @fig-06-07 shows the trial balance and the common-size income statement for fiscal 2026. Two checks tie the statement to the ledger. Net income equals the amount that the 2026 closing entry moved to retained earnings, and the balance sheet balances once net income is added to equity. Exercise 6.1 walks you through building both.

![From the Trial Balance to the Income Statement.](/visuals/svg/fig-06-07-ledger-to-income-statement.svg){#fig-06-07 fig-alt="A mock of two worksheets. The TrialBalance worksheet holds an Excel Table with one row for each account, showing the account number, name, subtype, and a debit or credit balance, with its first rows for cash, receivables, and inventories and a Total Row in which the debit and credit balances are equal, outlined. Below, the IncomeStatement worksheet shows fiscal 2026 operating revenue, sales returns, net revenue, cost of goods sold, gross margin, operating expenses, operating income, other income and expense, and net income, each with its percentage of net revenue. The formula bar shows the SUMIFS formula for operating revenue, and the net income row is outlined."}

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
A trial balance built from a ledger extract is only as complete as the extract. The Charles River ledger already holds supplier payments dated in fiscal 2027, so a trial balance without a date filter would mix two years. Filter by posting date before you group, and check the result: equal debit and credit balances show that the entries balance, but only a comparison with an independent figure, such as the closing entry, shows that nothing is missing.
:::


## From Description to Diagnosis

Tutorial 6.2 confirms what the Part I case found for Furniture, whose margin fell from the third quarter of fiscal 2026 to the fourth, and it adds that the other product lines held steady. That is a descriptive finding. The diagnostic question is why, and three moves answer it. The first is to drill down, from a total into its parts. Double-clicking a value in a PivotTable opens a new worksheet with the rows behind it, and moving a more detailed field, such as ProductType, into the Rows area splits a total into its components. The second is to compare, with the previous period, the same period a year earlier, a budget, or a peer group. The third is to decompose the change into components that add up exactly to it, so that each component can be assigned a cause.

### Explaining a Change in Margin

Gross margin is revenue minus cost, and revenue is the number of units sold multiplied by the price per unit. Between two periods, the margin of a product line can change for four reasons. More or fewer units can be sold, which is a volume effect. The sales can shift between items that earn different margins, which is a mix effect. The same items can be sold at different prices, which is a price effect. And the same items can cost more or less, which is a cost effect. Management accountants measure these effects against a budget as sales variances, splitting the effect of volume into a sales-quantity variance, from the change in the total number of units, and a sales-mix variance, from the shift between products (Datar & Rajan, 2021). The same logic works with the previous quarter as the benchmark, which is what the controller's question asks for.

The Charles River data lets you measure price precisely, because every invoice line records the item's list price as well as the price actually billed. The difference between the two has two parts, which Chapter 4 introduced: the reductions of the segment and customer price lists and approved overrides, and the promotional discounts recorded in the Discount column. Per unit sold, the margin is therefore the list margin, which is the list price minus the standard cost, less the price-list reductions and less the promotional discounts. @tbl-06-03 turns that identity into a bridge, and every input it needs is a total that a PivotTable can provide.

| Effect | What it measures | Calculation, Q3 to Q4 |
|---|---|---|
| Volume | The change in units, at the third quarter's margin per unit | `(U4-U3)*M3` |
| Mix | The change in list margin per unit, because different items were sold | `U4*(LM4-LM3)` |
| Price: price lists | The change in price-list reductions per unit | `-U4*(K4-K3)` |
| Price: promotions | The change in promotional discounts per unit | `-U4*(D4-D3)` |
| Cost | The change in each item's standard cost | Zero when no standard cost changes |

: The effects of a margin bridge. U is units sold, M the margin per unit, LM the list margin per unit, K the price-list reduction per unit, and D the promotional discount per unit, with 3 and 4 marking the quarters {#tbl-06-03}

The effects add up exactly to the fourth quarter's margin minus the third's, and checking that they do is the bridge's control total. The mix effect deserves a word. Because each item's list price and standard cost stay the same from one quarter to the next, the list margin per unit of a product line can change only when the items sold change, so its change isolates mix. The cost effect is zero for a related reason. InvoiceLines values every quantity at the item's standard cost, and each item has a single standard cost, so a margin at standard cost cannot move because of cost. Differences between actual and standard costs are recorded separately in the ledger, in variance accounts such as Manufacturing Variance, when work orders close. If a cost effect were the suspected cause, that is where you would look next.

A decomposition also depends on the level at which it is calculated. The bridge in @tbl-06-03 treats Furniture as a whole, so its mix effect captures every shift between Furniture items. Calculated product type by product type, the same change divides differently, because each type contains items with different prices and costs, and part of what looks like a change in price or cost at that level is really a change in the items sold within each type. Neither calculation is wrong, but a report should state its level, and Exercise 6.4 asks you to compare the two.

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
Management reports rarely present a variance without an explanation. A typical monthly or quarterly package shows each significant variance, its components, and a short commentary that names the cause and, where one is needed, the action and its owner, such as "Furniture margin 1.5 points below last quarter: promotional discounts; the promotion has ended." A bridge makes that commentary checkable, because each sentence rests on a number that ties to the total.
:::


{{< include _tutorial-03.qmd >}}


## Interpreting and Communicating Results

A PivotTable is a data product. A sentence that states what it shows, how you know, and what should happen next is an analytical finding, and the move from one to the other is where professional judgment enters. For the controller, the finding is short: the Furniture margin at standard cost fell by about a point and a half because promotional discounts more than doubled, while volume, list prices, the mix of items, and standard costs changed very little. The evidence is the bridge, which ties to the change in margin, and the drill-down by promotion, which names the Furniture Seasonal Promotion as the main source of the discounts.

Interpretation starts from an expectation. Auditors formalize this in substantive analytical procedures, analytical procedures used as evidence about whether an amount is misstated. The auditing standard of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) defines analytical procedures as comparisons of recorded amounts, or of ratios calculated from them, with expectations that the auditor develops from plausible relationships. It asks the auditor to decide in advance how large a difference from the expectation can be accepted without further investigation, and to evaluate significant unexpected differences, for example by reconsidering the expectation and by inquiring of management (PCAOB, n.d.). Management reporting benefits from the same discipline. Decide what you expect, and why, before you read the result, and treat a difference as a question to answer rather than a number to report.

A finding should also claim no more than its evidence supports. The bridge shows how much the discounts reduced the margin. It does not show whether the promotion was a good decision, because that depends on what the promotion achieved, such as sales it may have brought in, and on what the company intended. The quantities on the invoice lines, as you found in Chapter 5, are often fractional even for items sold by the unit. Per-unit measures calculated from totals are consistent from one quarter to the next, so they support the comparison, but a finding should not depend on whole units. Finally, match precision to the reader: a workpaper reconciles to the cent, while a memo to management rounds to the nearest thousand dollars or tenth of a percentage point.

::: {.callout-note .connecting-dots icon=false}
## Connecting the Dots
Every summary in this chapter has an equivalent in the tools of Parts III and IV. A PivotTable of revenue by product line and quarter is a SQL query that groups rows and sums them, and a calculated field is a measure defined on totals, which is how Power BI calculates margins. The waterfall chart of Tutorial 6.3 is one of the visual forms you will meet again when you study how to present results. The questions stay the same across the tools: which rows are included, at what level the numbers are totaled, and whether the parts add up to the whole.
:::


## Looking Ahead

This chapter has taken the controller's question from description to diagnosis. You profiled the fiscal 2026 invoice lines with statistical functions, learned why the mean and the median tell different stories about a skewed population, and drew the skew as a histogram. You calculated totals by category with conditional aggregation and used a control total to catch a category that was missing. You built PivotTables, added calculated fields that work on totals, displayed the same values as shares and changes, charted them, and learned to refresh and reference them safely. You grouped the general ledger into a pre-closing trial balance and turned it into a common-size income statement that ties to the closing entry. Finally, you drilled into the Furniture margin and decomposed its change into volume, mix, price, and cost effects that add up exactly to the change.

The analysis has answered the question that opened Part I. The Furniture margin fell because promotional discounts, mostly from the Furniture Seasonal Promotion, more than doubled from the third quarter to the fourth, and many of the promotion's orders were invoiced after it ended. Knowing why the margin fell is the starting point for deciding what to do about it, and Chapter 7 turns from explaining what happened to estimating what could happen next.
